theoryAdd.text: The half-power frequencies come from setting the net reactance equal to R, so that |Z| = √2 R. For a series circuit this gives ωL − 1/(ωC) = ±R, a quadratic in ω whose two positive roots are ω₁ and ω₂. Subtracting the two equations shows ω₂ − ω₁ = R/L exactly, which is why BW = R/(2πL) holds for any Q. Multiplying them shows ω₁ω₂ = 1/(LC) = ω₀², so the resonant frequency is the geometric mean of f₁ and f₂, and the curve is only symmetric about f_r when Q is high (about 10 or more).

theoryAdd.plainText: fr = √(f1 f2); Q = 2π × energy stored / energy lost per cycle

theoryAdd.text: At resonance energy swings back and forth between the magnetic field of L and the electric field of C, and the total stored energy stays constant at ½ L I_m² = ½ C V_Cm². The source only has to replace the energy burnt in R, which is I²R per second. The ratio of stored energy to energy lost per cycle, multiplied by 2π, is the general definition of Q; for a series circuit it reduces to ω₀L/R, and it also equals the ratio of the reactive power in L (or C) to the active power in R.

A practical tank circuit is a coil (L in series with its resistance R) in parallel with C. Making the admittance purely real gives a resonant frequency slightly below the ideal value, and resonance exists only if R < √(L/C). At that frequency the impedance is L/(CR) = Q²R, where Q = ω₀L/R is the coil Q. For the ideal three-branch parallel RLC circuit the roles of R are reversed: Q = R√(C/L) and BW = 1/(2πRC), so a larger parallel resistance gives a sharper response.

theoryAdd.plainText: Coil in parallel with C: fr = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²)

rows: Lower coil Q, lower Z_r, wider BW
Current in L and C branches

theoryAdd.text:
Example 2: coil L = 500 µH, R = 25 Ω, in parallel with C = 500 pF, V = 10 V
Ideal f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 5 × 10⁻⁷) = 318.3 kHz
R²/L² = 2.5 × 10⁹, tiny beside 1/(LC) = 4 × 10¹², so f_r ≈ 318.2 kHz
Q = ω0 L / R = (2 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻⁴)/25 = 40
Z_r = L/(CR) = 5 × 10⁻⁴/(5 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 25) = 40 kΩ (= Q²R)
Line current = 10 V / 40 kΩ = 0.25 mA
Capacitor current ≈ V ω0 C = 10 × 2 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 10 mA = Q × 0.25 mA

items: Using BW = R/L and calling it hertz: R/L is the bandwidth in rad/s; divide by 2π for Hz.
Taking f_r as the arithmetic mean of f₁ and f₂; it is the geometric mean, and the difference matters when Q is low.
Applying the series formulas Q = (1/R)√(L/C) and BW = R/(2πL) to a three-branch parallel circuit, where Q = R√(C/L).
Forgetting that a parallel circuit is inductive below f_r and capacitive above it, the reverse of a series circuit.
Using rms current in ½ L I² when the peak stored energy is asked for.

theoryAdd.text: Quick checks: at f_r, X_L = X_C = √(L/C); Q (series) = √(L/C)/R; BW = f_r/Q. If an answer for f_r changes when only R changes (series circuit), a formula has been misapplied.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF. Its resonant frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(10⁻² × 10⁻⁶)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1592 Hz ≈ 1.59 kHz. Leaving out 2π gives 10 kHz; leaving out the square root gives 15.9 MHz.

questions.questionText: Below its resonant frequency, a series RLC circuit behaves as:
options: An inductive circuit, with current lagging the voltage
A purely resistive circuit, with current in phase with the voltage
A capacitive circuit, with current leading the voltage
A capacitive circuit, with current lagging the voltage
questions.explanation: Below f_r, X_C = 1/(ωC) is larger than X_L = ωL, so the net reactance is capacitive and the current leads the voltage.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 20 Ω is at resonance, where X_L = X_C = 50 Ω. With a 100 V supply, the current is:
questions.explanation: At resonance the reactances cancel, so Z = R = 20 Ω and I = V/R = 100/20 = 5 A.

questions.questionText: In a series RLC circuit, the impedance at each half-power frequency is equal to:
questions.explanation: At a half-power frequency the current is I_max/√2, so the impedance is √2 times its minimum value R; there |X_L − X_C| = R.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.4 H and C = 10 µF. Its quality factor is:
A parallel resonant circuit is also known as a:
questions.explanation: At parallel resonance the impedance is maximum and the line current minimum, so the circuit rejects (blocks) the resonant frequency.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 20 Ω and L = 0.1 H. Its bandwidth is approximately:
questions.explanation: BW = R/(2πL) = 20/(2π × 0.1) ≈ 31.8 Hz. R/L = 200 is the bandwidth in rad/s, not in Hz.

questions.questionText: A series resonant circuit has f_r = 10 kHz and Q = 50. Its bandwidth is:
The quality factor Q of a resonant circuit is measured in:
options: No unit; it is a dimensionless ratio
questions.explanation: Q is a ratio of like quantities (reactance to resistance, or energy stored to energy lost), so it has no unit.

questions.questionText: A series circuit with R = 10 Ω, L = 50 mH and C = 0.5 µF is connected to a 10 V supply at its resonant frequency. The voltage across the inductor is approximately:
questions.explanation: At resonance X_L = √(L/C) = √(0.05/(0.5 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ 316 Ω and I = V/R = 1 A, so V_L = I X_L ≈ 316 V (Q ≈ 31.6 times the supply).

questions.questionText: In a series RLC circuit, R is increased while L and C are kept constant. Which quantity remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) does not contain R. Raising R lowers Q and the peak current and widens the bandwidth.

questions.questionText: Current magnification occurs in:
options: A series resonant circuit, where the line current is Q times V/R
A series resonant circuit, where the current in L is Q times the current in C
Any RC circuit driven above its corner frequency
A parallel resonant circuit, where each branch current can be Q times the line current
questions.explanation: In a parallel resonant circuit the L and C branch currents are nearly equal and opposite, each about Q times the small line current. Series resonance gives voltage magnification instead.

questions.questionText: A resonant circuit with a higher Q has:
options: A wider bandwidth and higher selectivity
A narrower bandwidth and lower selectivity
A narrower bandwidth and higher selectivity
A higher resonant frequency with the same bandwidth
questions.explanation: BW = f_r/Q, so a higher Q gives a narrower bandwidth, which means the circuit discriminates more sharply between nearby frequencies (higher selectivity).

questions.questionText: A series LC circuit resonates at 1 kHz. If the capacitance is made four times larger with L unchanged, the new resonant frequency is:
questions.explanation: f_r ∝ 1/√C, so multiplying C by 4 divides f_r by √4 = 2: 1000/2 = 500 Hz.

questions.questionText: What capacitance must be placed in series with a 0.5 H inductor to give resonance at 50 Hz?
A 253 pF capacitor is to resonate at 1 MHz. The inductance required is approximately:
A series resonant circuit has f_r = 455 kHz and Q = 50. Its half-power frequencies are approximately:
questions.explanation: BW = f_r/Q = 455/50 = 9.1 kHz. For a high-Q circuit f₁ ≈ f_r − BW/2 = 450.45 kHz and f₂ ≈ f_r + BW/2 = 459.55 kHz.

questions.questionText: The half-power frequencies of a series RLC circuit are 40 kHz and 90 kHz. The resonant frequency and the quality factor are:
questions.explanation: For a series RLC circuit f_r is the geometric mean: f_r = √(f₁f₂) = √(40 × 90) = 60 kHz. BW = 50 kHz, so Q = f_r/BW = 60/50 = 1.2. The arithmetic mean (65 kHz) is only an approximation for high Q.

questions.questionText: A coil of inductance 0.2 H and resistance 20 Ω is connected in parallel with a 10 µF capacitor across a 200 V supply at the resonant frequency. The line current is:
questions.explanation: Dynamic impedance Z_r = L/(CR) = 0.2/(10⁻⁵ × 20) = 1000 Ω, so the line current is 200/1000 = 0.2 A.

questions.questionText: A coil with L = 0.1 H and R = 60 Ω is connected in parallel with a 10 µF capacitor. The resonant frequency of the combination is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_r = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²) = (1/2π)√(10⁶ − 3.6 × 10⁵) = 800/(2π) ≈ 127 Hz, lower than the ideal value 1/(2π√(LC)) ≈ 159 Hz because of the coil resistance.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF. When it is supplied at twice its resonant frequency, its impedance and nature are:
questions.explanation: At f_r, X_L = X_C = √(L/C) = 100 Ω. At 2f_r, X_L = 200 Ω and X_C = 50 Ω, so Z = √(10² + 150²) ≈ 150 Ω; X_L > X_C, so the circuit is inductive.

questions.questionText: An ideal parallel RLC circuit (R, L and C each in a separate branch) has R = 10 kΩ, L = 1 mH and C = 10 nF. Its quality factor and bandwidth are:
questions.explanation: For the three-branch parallel circuit Q = R√(C/L) = 10⁴ × √(10⁻⁵) ≈ 31.6 and BW = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.59 kHz. The series formulas (1/R)√(L/C) and R/(2πL) do not apply here.

questions.questionText: A coil of inductance 2 mH and resistance 25 Ω is used at 100 kHz. Its quality factor at this frequency is approximately:
In terms of energy, the quality factor of a resonant circuit is defined as:
options: (maximum energy stored) / (2π × energy dissipated per cycle)
questions.explanation: Q = 2π × W_stored/W_lost per cycle. For a series circuit this reduces to ω₀L/R, the familiar X_L/R.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 50 Ω is fed from a 100 V variable-frequency supply. The power dissipated at either half-power frequency is:
questions.explanation: Maximum power at resonance is V²/R = 100²/50 = 200 W. At a half-power frequency it is half of this, 100 W.

questions.questionText: The maximum current of a series RLC circuit at resonance is 4 A. The current at the lower half-power frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: At a half-power frequency I = I_max/√2 = 4 × 0.707 ≈ 2.83 A, which makes the power I²R exactly half the maximum.

questions.questionText: At the upper half-power frequency of a series RLC circuit, the current:
options: Is in phase with the supply voltage
questions.explanation: Above f_r the circuit is inductive, and at f₂ the net reactance X_L − X_C equals R, so tan φ = 1 and the current lags by 45°.

questions.questionText: At series resonance, the net voltage across the series L-C combination (measured across both together) is:
options: Zero, because V_L and V_C are equal and 180° apart
questions.explanation: V_L and V_C are each Q × V but in antiphase, so their phasor sum is zero and the whole supply voltage appears across R.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 5 Ω resonates at 1 kHz. With 10 V applied at resonance, the voltage across the capacitor is 250 V. The inductance is approximately:
questions.explanation: I = V/R = 10/5 = 2 A, so X_C = V_C/I = 125 Ω. At resonance X_L = X_C = 125 Ω, so L = 125/(2π × 1000) ≈ 19.9 mH (Q = 25).

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit must resonate at 10 kHz with a bandwidth of 100 Hz using a 10 mH inductor. The required R and C are approximately:
A radio tuning circuit uses a fixed inductor with a variable capacitor adjustable from 30 pF to 300 pF. The ratio of the highest to the lowest resonant frequency is approximately:
A tuned circuit with a fixed inductor must cover 550 kHz to 1650 kHz. The ratio C_max/C_min of the variable capacitor must be:
questions.explanation: C ∝ 1/f², so C_max/C_min = (f_max/f_min)² = (1650/550)² = 3² = 9.

questions.questionText: A parallel tank circuit with Q = 40 draws a line current of 5 mA at resonance. The current in the capacitor branch is approximately:
questions.explanation: At parallel resonance each branch current is about Q times the line current: I_C ≈ 40 × 5 mA = 200 mA.

questions.questionText: A coil (L = 200 µH, R = 10 Ω) is connected in parallel with a 200 pF capacitor. Its resonant frequency and dynamic impedance are approximately:
questions.explanation: Since R² ≪ L/C, f_r ≈ 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 2 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 796 kHz. Z_r = L/(CR) = 200 × 10⁻⁶/(200 × 10⁻¹² × 10) = 100 kΩ (equivalently Q²R with Q = 100). 5 MHz is ω₀ in rad/s, not f.

questions.questionText: Which statement about series resonance is NOT correct?
options: The current is in phase with the supply voltage
Increasing R raises the resonant frequency
The voltages across L and C can each exceed the supply voltage
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) is independent of R. The other statements are all true at series resonance.

questions.questionText: In an ideal (lossless) parallel LC circuit at resonance:
options: The line current is zero although the branch currents are not
The branch currents are both zero
questions.explanation: The inductor and capacitor currents are equal in magnitude and 180° apart, so they cancel at the junction; the impedance is infinite and no current is drawn from the supply.

questions.questionText: A wave trap is used to block one interfering frequency from reaching a receiver. It is:
options: A series LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected in series with the signal path
A parallel LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected in series with the signal path
A parallel LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected across the signal path
A resistor connected in series with the signal path
questions.explanation: A parallel resonant circuit has maximum impedance at its resonant frequency, so placed in series with the line it blocks that frequency while passing others.

questions.questionText: An ideal parallel LC circuit is operated above its resonant frequency. It behaves as:
options: An inductive load, because X_L is larger than X_C
A capacitive load, because the capacitor branch draws the larger current
An inductive load, because the inductor branch draws the larger current
questions.explanation: Above f_r, X_C is smaller than X_L, so the capacitor branch current dominates and the net line current leads: the parallel circuit looks capacitive (the opposite of a series circuit).

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω has a bandwidth of 50 Hz. If R is increased to 25 Ω with L and C unchanged, the new bandwidth is:
questions.explanation: BW = R/(2πL) is proportional to R: 50 × (25/10) = 125 Hz.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and L = 20 mH is supplied with 20 V (rms) at its resonant frequency. The maximum energy stored in the inductor is:
questions.explanation: I = V/R = 2 A rms, so I_m = 2√2 A. W = ½ L I_m² = ½ × 0.02 × 8 = 0.08 J. Using the rms current gives 0.04 J.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 100 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF. Its exact upper half-power frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: ω₂ = R/(2L) + √((R/2L)² + 1/(LC)) = 500 + √(250 000 + 10⁶) ≈ 1618 rad/s, so f₂ ≈ 257.5 Hz. Q = 1 here, so f_r + BW/2 ≈ 238.7 Hz is not accurate.

questions.questionText: A resonant circuit has f_r = 2 MHz and a bandwidth of 40 kHz. Its quality factor is:
A practical coil (L with series resistance R) is connected in parallel with a capacitor C. Resonance (unity power factor) is possible only if:
options: R has any value, because the resonant frequency does not depend on R
questions.explanation: f_r = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²) is real only when 1/(LC) > R²/L², that is R < √(L/C).
